Although some forms of epilepsy may respond to surgical treatment and others may not require any treatment at all, most o patients with epilepsy require appropriate pharmacological therapy (Perucca, 1996). In the past i decade, several new options for the medical treatment of epilepsy have been introduced, z including novel AEDs and vagus nerve stimulation. i The newer AEDs differ from older agents in several important ways, including mechanism of action, spectrum of activity, and pharmacokinetic (PK) characteristics (Herman and u Pedley, 1998). However, more than 30% of patients have inadequate seizure control on currently f available AEDs or experience significant adverse drug effects (Beghi and Sander, 2008). e Therefore, a need remains for AEDs with improved effectiveness and tolerability i e (Shorvon, 2009). Lacosamide P has also been i shown to be an effective and safe adjunctive treatment over the O long term (up to 9 years) for study participants with POS. Use of a loading dose for initiation C of adjunctive o LCM treatment (single loading dose of LCM 200mg, followed approximately 12 hours later p by LCM o 100mg twice daily [200mg/day] maintenance dose regimen) is approved in the EU, US, and s other countries. In the US, oral tablets and oral solution (syrup) of LCM are indicated for the treatment of POS in patients ≥4 years of age. Additionally, LCM t has been approved in the EU (oral tablets, oral P n solution, and solution for intravenous [iv] d infusion), e as monotherapy and adjunctive therapy in the treatment of POS with or without secondary x generalization in patients ≥4 years of age. text: Lacosamide o a is a member of a series of functionalized amino acids that were specifically d synthesized as anticonvulsive drug candidates. Lacosamide’s mode of action is proposed to be s mediated by a selective enhancement of slow inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels h which may explain the anticonvulsant effects of LCM (Rogawski et al, 2015; Niespodziany et al, 2012; Errington et al, 2007). As of 31 Aug 2019, LCM has been approved in over 70 countries. Lacosamide has been approved as monotherapy and adjunctive treatment in patients with POS in the US (4 years and older for film-coated tablets and oral solution; 17 years of age and older for intravenous [iv] infusion), Canada (18 years and older for film-coated tablets and iv infusion), EU (4 years and older for film-coated tablets, oral solution, and iv infusion), and Japan (4 years and older for film-coated tablets, dry syrup, and iv infusion). Currently, LCM is still under development for use as monotherapy in other regions and also as iv administration in patients with POS, for n monotherapy and adjunctive therapy in pediatric patients ≥1 month to <4 years of age with epilepsy, and as adjunctive therapy for primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures in adult and a pediatric patients ≥4 years of age with idiopathic generalized epilepsy. In the clinical development program for LCM, safety and tolerability of multiple doses of up to LCM 400mg given twice daily (LCM 800mg/day) were evaluated in approximately 700 t study participants who received LCM in Phase 1 studies. Lacosamide is rapidly and completely a . absorbed after oral administration and has minimal protein-binding properties, thus g a low risk of displacement drug-drug interactions. Lacosamide is neither a strong inhibitor nor n a known inducer of the CYP450 enzymes and hence has a low potential for drug-drug t interactions. Food does not affect the rate and extent of absorption. Peak plasma concentrations k occur t between 0.5 and 4 hours after dosing. The PK properties of LCM are proportional a to dose, with low intraparticipant and interparticipant variability. The terminal half-life of the o unchanged drug in plasma is approximately 13 hours allowing for a twice-daily dose y regimen. t The O-desmethyl metabolite (referred to as SPM 12809) is excreted in P the urine, represents i about 30% of the dose, and has no known pharmacological activity. After O single-dose administration in healthy study participants, bioequivalence has been shown C between o the tablet and solution for iv infusion as well as between the tablet and oral solution formulations. p o Further information on LCM preclinical L results, as well n as the PK, efficacy, and safety profiles, can be obtained from the current version of the LCM Investigator’s Brochure.

breadcrumb: 2 INTRODUCTION > 2.2 Background l > 2.2.1 Lacosamide in pediatric t studies n
text: Pellock et al (2012) conducted a systematic review of AEDs used in the treatment of POS. The AEDs that were shown to be superior u to placebo e for the adjunctive treatment of POS in adult clinical studies were also shown e to be superior y to placebo for adjunctive treatment of POS in the pediatric clinical studies (study b participants >2 years of age) in which they were investigated. The efficacy and safety of t LCM observed in clinical studies in adults and preclinical data, as well as many additional n attributes n of LCM, render the drug appropriate to investigate in pediatric study participants. These attributes include predictable and linear PK, lack of drug-drug interactions, easy twice daily n dosing, and the availability of 3 different types of formulations in multiple strengths t (allowing i for flexibility in dose range and individualizing treatment). Given the demonstrated c efficacy and safety of LCM as adjunctive treatment in study participants aged ≥16 years l with POS, and the experience with other AEDs in pediatric study participants, the c US Food p and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Authority (EMA) determined that it is acceptable to extrapolate the effectiveness of drugs approved for the treatment of POS in adults to pediatrics. UCB chose to utilize extrapolation of efficacy from i adults to the pediatric population (≥4 years of age) for the indication of POS in the US and the T EU. Based on this extrapolation, the EMA approved this indication on 14 Sep 2017, and the US FDA approved this indication (tablets and oral solution only) on 03 Nov 2017. Lacosamide is being evaluated in pediatric study participants ≥1 month to ≤17 years of age with seizures in completed and ongoing studies. The completed pediatric studies include SP847 (open-label, safety, tolerability, and PK study) and SP1047 (PK study for study participants prescribed LCM); ongoing pediatric studies include SP848 and EP0034 (open-label, long-term safety studies). In SP847, SP848, and EP0034, study participants with POS have received LCM oral solution at doses up to 12mg/kg/day based on tolerability. In SP1047, study participants with n epilepsy received LCM oral tablets (50mg, 100mg, 150mg, or 200mg), or LCM oral solution (LCM 10mg/mL) that they had been prescribed for epilepsy and brought with them to the clinic a for dosing. Preliminary data have not demonstrated any clinically relevant changes in vital signs, electrocardiograms (ECGs), or clinical laboratory values; or evidence of cardiac-related o treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) or body weight changes. SP0967 is an ongoing Phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, randomized, PBO-controlled, parallel-group study u to evaluate the efficacy and safety of LCM oral solution (LCM 8mg/kg/day to 12mg/kg/day, or matching f PBO) as adjunctive therapy in study participants ≥1 month to <4 years of age with POS. e SP0967 has completed enrollment, and no safety issues have been identified by safety i monitoring e and an external Data Monitoring Committee. EP0060 is a completed study that evaluated the safety and tolerability of the LCM iv formulation (infusion duration 15 minutes to r 60 minutes) s in children with epilepsy ≥1 month to <17 years of age. Lacosamide was well m tolerated in that study and no safety issues were identified. i
